item.title: Hastie ‘open minded’ on return of baby bonus to counter ageing population concerns – as it happened
item.description:
This blog is now closed

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Dan Tehan says fuel excise cut when oil price high a ‘sensible’ plan

Dan Tehan, the shadow minister for energy, said Gallagher’s criticism of the Coalition’s fuel plan wasn’t fair.

[What] I would say to Anthony Albanese and the Labor party is get out amongst the people and see what’s happening in your electorates because people are hurting because of cost of living …

We have the discipline to be able to do the policy work to make sure we can offset policies like this so it won’t be inflationary and it will provide much needed relief to people, and they need it now.

Obviously we’ve helped when the war started with some changes to the fuel excise but we’ve shifted, and [are] including in the budget, to providing more permanent cost of living arrangements, including through the tax system, to make sure that that ongoing cost-of-living help is there permanently, not just in these one-off arrangements, which, when we’ve got higher inflation, could be difficult in the economy.

Our decisions have been built and baked into the budget to make sure that that cost-of-living help is permanent. You know, the sooner this war in the Middle East stops, the better.

item.title: Middle East braces for more violence as Iran claims US is planning to renew bombing campaign
item.description:
Tensions grow as Trump tells Fox News he is considering ‘wiping Iran out’ after attacks on Riyadh by Houthi rebels

Governments across the Middle East are bracing for an escalation of violence after Iran claimed it had received intelligence that the US was preparing for a renewed bombing campaign against the Islamic Republic.

In a potential sign of growing tensions before the UN general assembly in New York this week, Donald Trump cut short a weekend visit to the Camp David presidential retreat on Sunday with no official explanation, and a new security alert was issued by the state department to all US citizens in the Middle East.

item.title: Thick smoke seen near Riyadh airport as Houthis claim attack on Saudi capital
item.description:
Authorities issued warnings for city in first such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with Iran-backed Houthis escalated in July

Yemen’s Houthis said they attacked “sensitive” sites in the Saudi capital with missiles and drones, hours after flames and a large plume of black smoke were seen rising above Riyadh airport on Saturday.

The Saudi government sent air raid alerts to citizens by phone overnight warning of aerial attacks, marking the first time the government has issued such alerts for Riyadh since fighting with the Iran-backed Houthis escalated in July.

item.title: Yemen’s anti-Houthi forces launch inquest into sudden military collapse
item.description:
Rout raises questions about coordination and morale as some politicians claim billions of dollars were offered to persuade forces to abandon position

A bitter inquest is under way among Yemen’s anti-Houthi forces as to how what was being billed as a decisive assault on Sana’a, the Houthi-controlled capital, suddenly collapsed into a military rout.

More than 15 brigades were defeated as the country’s entire west coast fell into Houthi hands. Efforts are now being made to reorganise the anti-Houthi forces representing the UN-recognised Yemeni government in order to capture the Kahbob mountains, a strategic point from which to restrict Houthi forces moving closer to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait.

item.title: Nvidia boss says there is ‘0% chance’ AI destroys the world by 2030
item.description:
Jensen Huang dismisses warnings from former Anthropic researcher and others as ‘doomsday narratives’

  • Business live – latest updates

The boss of the chipmaker Nvidia has said AI will not develop to a point that will lead to the extinction of the human race within a few years, rejecting such assertions as overblown “doomsday narratives”.

Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of the $5tn AI chipmaker, said the claims made on social media by the former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon that AI could become “superhuman” and kill off humanity within the decade were “irresponsible”.

item.title: Yemen's Houthis are upending the Gulf order. The Saudis are the biggest losers
item.description:
Yemen's Houthis are upending the Gulf order. The Saudis are the biggest losers

Submitted by Joe Gill on Fri, 09/18/2026 - 20:05
The war has entered a critical phase, with the Iran-aligned group calling the shots, as Trump leaves Mohammed bin Salman out in the cold
Houthi supporters carry a portrait of the leader of the group, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, in a protest denouncing Saudi Arabia’s aggression against Yemen, in Sanaa, on 18 September 2026 (Mohammed Huwais/AFP)
Off

A ballistic missile strike hits a fuel depot close to Riyadh’s international airport. Air raid sirens wailed across the Saudi capital before dawn on Saturday, as they did across other regions, including Jeddah, Taif and Yanbu.

The Houthi strikes exposed how vulnerable the Gulf kingdom is to the Yemeni group’s recent wave of attacks on the country, which they say are a response to Saudi strikes on Yemen. 

Will US President Donald Trump assist his friend Mohammed bin Salman? The crown prince - who the US president failed to help when oil terminals were hit by missiles from Iraq in 2019 - called the White House asking for US support in its war with Ansar Allah (Houthis). Once again, Trump said no.

The $600bn that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman committed to investing in the US in his deals with Trump last year has bought almost zero protection from the world’s military superpower.

The administration offered to share intelligence and assist Riyadh with targeting operations, but Trump desperately wants to avoid opening any new fronts, with US forces overstretched in the blockade of Iran.

Instead, Trump made a deal with the group that had fought the Saudi coalition to a standstill in Yemen after a devastating eight-year war. Under the terms recently agreed in Muscat, Houthi leaders confirmed they would uphold a 2025 ceasefire with the US, ensuring the Red Sea remains open to global shipping, except for Saudi vessels. 

In sum, the Houthis would continue the war with Saudi Arabia, and the US would stay out of it. Mohammed bin Salman was politely thrown under the bus.

Meanwhile, military commanders from the US and aligned Arab states were reportedly brought together with their Israeli counterparts in Germany - a secret meeting organised by US Central Command (Centcom) to discuss the Iran war. Israel then leaked the meeting.

Sources told Israeli journalist Barak Ravid that the “private retreat” was organised by Centcom commander Admiral Brad Cooper, and attended by the military chiefs of staff of Israel, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt.

Unreliable partners

Any time Arab states secretly meet with Israeli officials, they should by now realise that it will not remain so, due to Israel’s predilection for boasting. Israel doesn’t do discreet diplomacy. It’s no secret that pro-western Arab states have been doing under-the-counter deals with “the Zionist entity” for decades.

Earlier this month, Houthi fighters launched a rapid assault from southern Hodeidah and western Taiz, capturing the Red Sea port of Mocha overnight. They then advanced to capture the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and Perim Island - a strategic point overseeing the vital waterway - as Saudi-backed government troops withdrew. 

Washington is not yet ready to treat its opponents as sovereign states with legitimate interests, and to cut lasting deals with them

The fighting was bloody. Anti-Houthi National Resistance Forces reported that more than 500 of their fighters were killed and 1,500 injured. Clashes continue near Mocha and other fronts.

Saudi strikes on Yemen’s Houthi forces have been met with Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. The key East-West Pipeline to the Red Sea has been hit. But Riyadh’s new Mecca defence pact allies, Turkey and Pakistan, have not come to its aid.

If not them and not Washington, then who? 

Enter Benjamin Netanyahu, who has offered military and intelligence assistance to the Gulf states. Saudi Arabia is already getting intelligence from Israel via the US on the Yemenis. Still, Riyadh does not see Israel as a reliable military partner, says Gulf analyst Andreas Krieg. “Riyadh does not want to move from dependence on Washington to dependence on an Israeli security architecture,” he told The New Arab.

Fears that Iran's Yemeni allies will close off the main route for energy and shipping through the Red Sea, on top of the semi-paralysed Strait of Hormuz, have caused further spikes in oil and diesel prices.

A senior Israeli intelligence source told Al-Monitor: “At the moment, no one has deterrence over the Houthis. Not the Americans, not us, and certainly not the Saudis. They are the dark horse that no one expected.”

Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has agreed to send military advisers to Saudi Arabia, raising fears that the UK could once again be drawn into a Saudi war on Yemen.

Trump will not intervene for Mohammed bin Salman, but he will sell billions of dollars worth of F-35s and one-tonne bombs to Riyadh. The US has just signed off on massive shipments of bombs to both Israel and Saudi Arabia. 

For Saudi Arabia, the Trump administration approved a $5bn package including 10,000 JDAM guidance kits and 10,000 bombs, split evenly between 500lb munitions and 2,000lb BLU-117s. For Israel, the $2.8bn US taxpayer-funded shipment includes 40,000 bombs - half BLU-117s and half MK-84s - and 20,000 penetrator warheads for hardened targets. It is the largest single transfer of this type of bomb to Israel in years.

The scale of these planned shipments is terrifying, as American commentator Tucker Carlson recently pointed out, dwarfing the equivalent tonnage of the Second World War US bombings of Tokyo and Hiroshima. Like those airborne atrocities, the bombs will likely be used against defenceless civilians in Gaza, Lebanon and Yemen.

How to end the war

How can this latest escalation be brought to an end? Ansar Allah, which governs more than 70 percent of Yemen’s population, insists that the war can be stopped by lifting the 12-year-old Saudi blockade on Yemen.

Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a senior Houthi spokesperson, told Sky News that Sanaa was seeking “to end the blockade and to end the aggression against Yemenis … The ball is in the Saudis’ court; it is their decision to stop this war.”

He added: “All we have done is put the equation of a blockade for a blockade”, referring to the Saudi air, land and sea cordon around Yemen, which has starved its people and caused untold suffering, leading to tens of thousands of deaths.

Saudi-Yemen conflict: The notion of an 'American saviour' is dead
Read More »

In the words of US journalist Ryan Grim, the solution to the wider conflict is simple, if unpalatable for Washington: “End the wars and treat Yemen and Iran like sovereign nations with an equal place in the world. (And also stop Israel’s attacks on southern Lebanon.) That’s it. That’s basically all they’d have to do. Just stop insisting on domination.”

Put this way, it is extraordinary how the US can disguise its actions, and those of its allies, as defensive, when in fact it has been waging a decades-long war on Iran using sanctions, assassinations, sabotage and blockades. This conflict is now longer than the Cold War.

The US empire has yet to reach a point of realism, where it can retreat from its unbridled supremacy with grace. And yet, six weeks out from the midterm elections, Trump needs to find a way to wind down the Middle East war he helped start with Netanyahu, and to tamp down record fuel prices for Americans - hence the deal with the Houthis.

Washington is not yet ready to treat its opponents as sovereign states with legitimate interests, and to cut lasting deals with them. The June memorandum with Iran looked promising, but almost immediately, Trump ripped it up.

Yet after November’s midterm elections, when Republicans are likely to be punished for Trump’s war, that may begin to change. Trillion-dollar defence bills are piling up the national debt, while global holders of US treasuries are offloading them at a worrying rate. 

After the 2028 presidential election, perhaps Trump or his successor will do as former President Richard Nixon did, and make peace with Washington’s enemies. But they would have to cut Israel loose to do it.
